content.title: Choosing an Effective Introductory Sentence
content.overview: An effective introductory sentence establishes the paragraph's main topic and scope, acting as a bridge between the preceding text and the specific details that follow. On the ACT, you must select the sentence that best frames the paragraph's purpose without introducing irrelevant information or repeating specific details found later in the paragraph.
learning_objectives: Identify the main topic and scope of a paragraph based on its supporting details.
Select an introductory sentence that narrows from a general concept to a specific focus.
Eliminate introductory options that introduce unrelated topics or redundant information.
Verify that the chosen introduction logically leads into the first supporting detail.

sections.title: The Role of the Topic-Frame Intro
sections.content: The introductory sentence, often called the topic sentence, serves two primary functions: it identifies the subject matter and sets the 'angle' or scope of the discussion. A strong introduction often follows a 'general-to-specific' flow. It starts with a broader claim that encompasses the paragraph's theme and then narrows down to hint at the specific evidence or direction the paragraph will take. If a paragraph discusses the benefits of urban gardening, the intro should mention urban gardening generally, not just one specific type of tomato grown there.

sections.title: Matching Topic and Scope
sections.content: To choose the right sentence, you must analyze the entire paragraph first. Look at the supporting details. If the details focus on the economic impact of a new stadium, the introduction must mention economics or financial effects, not just the stadium's architecture. The scope must be 'just right'—neither so broad that it covers the whole essay nor so narrow that it only describes the very next sentence.

sections.title: Elimination Strategies
sections.content: ACT distractors for this topic usually fall into three categories: 1) Off-topic: The sentence introduces a new subject (e.g., cost) that the paragraph never addresses. 2) Too Narrow: The sentence focuses on a single detail (e.g., a specific tree species) when the paragraph is about the whole forest. 3) Redundant: The sentence repeats a specific fact that is already stated more effectively later in the paragraph.

worked_examples.question:
Context: ...Recent studies suggest city parks improve mental health. [X] The park’s walking trails, benches, and community events encourage social interaction and gentle exercise. Park maintenance and programming vary among neighborhoods, affecting who uses them and how often.

Which choice best replaces [X] as the introductory sentence for this paragraph?
A. City parks are expensive to build and maintain.
B. Access to green space can influence residents’ well-being and daily routines.
C. Many cities are redesigning parks with sports fields and playgrounds.
D. Trees provide shade and habitat, making parks more pleasant.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the paragraph's focus. The details discuss social interaction, exercise, and how maintenance affects usage. Step 2: Evaluate Choice A. It introduces 'cost,' which is never mentioned again. Eliminate. Step 3: Evaluate Choice B. It mentions 'well-being' (matching mental health) and 'daily routines' (matching walking and usage). This fits the scope. Step 4: Evaluate Choice C. It focuses on 'redesigning,' which is not the paragraph's focus. Eliminate. Step 5: Evaluate Choice D. It focuses only on 'trees,' which is too narrow for a paragraph about social interaction and programming. Correct Answer: B.

common_mistakes: Choosing a sentence that is true in the real world but not supported by the specific details in the paragraph.
Selecting a sentence that is too broad, covering the entire passage's theme rather than the specific paragraph's focus.
Picking a sentence that introduces a 'hook' or interesting fact that the rest of the paragraph fails to develop.
exam_tips: Always read the entire paragraph before looking at the answer choices for an introductory sentence.
Perform a 'Lead-in Check': Read your chosen sentence followed immediately by the next sentence in the paragraph to ensure the transition is logical.
Beware of choices that repeat the exact wording of the final sentence; an intro should set up the paragraph, not summarize the end.
content.recap: An effective introductory sentence frames the paragraph by matching its topic and scope. It should transition from a general idea to the specific focus developed by the supporting details while avoiding irrelevant new information.

knowledge_claims.content: An introductory sentence must identify the paragraph's main topic and its specific angle or scope.
To select the best intro, one must first identify the paragraph's main topic and scope from its existing sentence-level cues.
Effective introductory sentences typically narrow from a general claim to a specific focus that the paragraph then develops.
It is a mistake to choose an introductory sentence that introduces a new, unrelated topic not discussed in the rest of the paragraph.
An introductory sentence should not repeat specific details that are already presented later in the paragraph.
A valid introductory sentence must lead logically into the paragraph's first supporting detail.
If a paragraph focuses on the social benefits of a location, the introductory sentence should frame the topic around social interaction or community impact.
An intro that is 'too narrow' focuses on a single detail, whereas an effective intro encompasses all the major points of the paragraph.
Distractor choices often use 'true' statements that are irrelevant to the specific paragraph's development.
When a paragraph discusses how maintenance affects usage, the intro should mention factors like access or daily routines.
The 'Lead-in Check' involves reading the chosen intro with the subsequent sentence to ensure a smooth flow of information.
The scope of the introductory sentence must match the breadth of the evidence provided in the paragraph.

items.stem:
Practice form 1. Rina is editing a short report about a community garden.

Which opening most effectively introduces the passage?
A) Projects exist in many places.
B) This passage has several paragraphs.
C) When a weekly survey revealed a recurring obstacle, volunteers tested a simple solution.
D) Many people have opinions about things.

options.C: When a weekly survey revealed a recurring obstacle, volunteers tested a simple solution.
options.D: Many people have opinions about things.

items.explanation: The correct choice directly applies the target skill: 选择有效的引言.
